transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, I suppose I should start by saying I’m a physical scientist, which means my work is highly structured, or at least it’s supposed to be. But lately, I just... I came in because I can't keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. It’s like my brain is a radio scanning every frequency at once. For example, just last week, we had this massive grant call—absolutely critical, millions of dollars on the line, everyone is stressed—and right in the middle of it, I noticed this faint vibration coming from one of the vacuum pumps down the hall. No one else seemed to hear it, but to me, it was deafening. Or we’ll be in a mandatory safety meeting, which I know I need to pay attention to, but a grad student will make some offhand comment about a calibration error, or I’ll remember some odd peak in an old spectrum from three years ago, and that’s it. Suddenly, I’m off chasing that for hours. I’ll pull up old data files, cross-reference them, start writing new protocols, completely consumed by it, while the thing everyone actually needs from me—the grant proposal, the safety sign-offs—just completely falls apart. It’s like I have no filter for what’s important and what’s not, and it’s causing absolute chaos in the lab. My PI is furious, and honestly, I don't blame him, because I know I should be focusing, but I literally just can't stop myself from getting derailed by every single little thing that crosses my path.
Has this kind of difficulty staying focused and getting pulled into tangents been something you've experienced since you were a child, or is this a new pattern that's developed more recently?

Oh, no, no, this is definitely new. I mean, I’ve always been someone who could hyper-focus when the work called for it—you kind of have to be in this field, honestly. When you’re running a 12-hour data collection shift, you need to be able to just lock in. So, no, as a kid, in college, even through most of my career, I was the one people relied on to stay on track. I was the organized one. 

But this... whatever this is, this absolute inability to filter out the noise and stay on task, it really started about seven months ago. I remember the timeline exactly because that’s when my PI asked me to take over the multi-site spectroscopy project. It was a huge step up in responsibility. We’re talking coordinating data from three different universities, managing a team of post-docs, ensuring all the equipment is calibrated across different labs... it’s a massive undertaking. And at first, I thought maybe I was just overwhelmed by the logistics of it all. You know, you get a new project, especially one with so many moving parts, and there’s a learning curve. You have to figure out how to juggle everything. 

But it didn't get better. It got worse. Instead of settling into a rhythm, I just started fracturing. Like I said, I'd be looking at a crucial spreadsheet for the multi-site project, something that needed to be sent to the collaborators that afternoon, and then I'd notice a discrepancy in a completely unrelated file from two years ago, and suddenly it's 3 AM and I've rewritten the entire data analysis protocol for a project that's already been published. So, yeah, seven months of this. Ever since I took over that spectroscopy project, my brain has just been... misfiring. It's like I have all this energy and drive, but no steering wheel whatsoever.
Along with this distractibility, have you also noticed changes like feeling unusually elated, energetic, or needing much less sleep than usual over these past seven months?

Well, yes, actually. The sleep thing is... it’s been one of the most bizarre parts of all this. Because, normally, I’m an eight-hours-a-night kind of person. If I didn't get my eight hours, I’d be dragging through the lab, drinking three cups of coffee just to calibrate the instruments. But for the last seven months? It’s like someone flipped a switch in my brain and decided that sleep is just this completely inefficient interruption to my day. 

Most nights, I’m only getting two, maybe three hours of sleep. Tops. And the crazy thing is, I’m not even going to bed properly. I’ll be on the couch, right? My laptop is open, I’ve got three different datasets pulled up, maybe a notepad with some equations I’m trying to balance, and I’ll just sort of... power down for a couple of hours right there. But then I wake up, and instead of feeling groggy or exhausted like a normal person would after sleeping on a couch for two hours, I am just incredibly sharp. I mean, my eyes open, and I am instantly ready to work. It’s like my brain never actually stopped; it just paused for a second. 

And the energy, oh my god, the energy. It’s relentless. I’ll wake up at 4 AM, and I won't even need coffee. I’ll just dive straight back into whatever I was doing, or I’ll start pacing around the living room thinking about how we can optimize the vacuum chamber seals, or I’ll start drafting emails to the post-docs that I have to schedule to send at 8 AM so I don’t look like an absolute lunatic. But I feel fantastic. I feel like I could run a marathon and then immediately go run a 24-hour experiment without breaking a sweat. It’s exhilarating, honestly, feeling this... this electric current just buzzing through me all day and all night, but I know it doesn't make sense to not be tired. I just... I don't feel tired. At all.

Before these last seven months, have you ever had a distinct period—lasting two weeks or more—where you felt unusually low, hopeless, or lost interest in things, or a separate earlier time when you felt abnormally elated or full of energy like this?

Well, no. No, I really haven't. I mean, I've always been pretty steady. You know, you have to be in this field. You can't just be bouncing off the walls or falling into some kind of pit of despair when you're trying to calibrate a mass spectrometer, right? So, no, I've never had anything like that. I mean, sure, there are times when an experiment fails, and you've spent three months on it, and you feel frustrated, maybe a little down for a day or two, but nothing like two whole weeks of just... hopelessness. I've always been able to bounce back, look at the data, figure out what went wrong, and just get back to work. 

And as for feeling like this before... no, absolutely not. This energy, this constant buzzing, it's completely new. Like I said, I was always the eight-hours-a-night person. I was the one who needed my routine. I'd wake up, have my coffee, read the journals, go to the lab, work my shift, come home, maybe watch a documentary, and go to sleep. It was very predictable. Very... baseline, I guess you could say. I never had these periods where I felt like I could conquer the world on two hours of sleep. I mean, if I had, I probably would have published twice as many papers by now, right? But no, this whole... whatever this is, this electric feeling, it really just started with that spectroscopy project seven months ago. Before that, I was just... me. Just a normal, slightly overworked scientist, but definitely not someone who felt like they were vibrating at a higher frequency than everyone else in the room. So, yeah, no history of anything like this, high or low. It's all just... very, very new.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a distinct 7-month period marked by abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive mood, markedly decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours with no fatigue), increased energy, distractibility, and excessive involvement in goal-directed activities (obsessive tangential research pursuits) causing significant impairment in occupational functioning.
